title: Working a health passage under time
blurb: Work a 250-500 word health passage and its question set at HESI pace: skim for gists, classify each stem, scan for key words and match every qualifier.
question: A HESI A2 passage of about 400 words on hydration in older adults is followed by six questions: main idea, two details, a word in context, an inference and the author's purpose. With about 65 seconds per item, how do you work the whole set without rereading the passage six times?

teach.h: One passage, a set of questions, one clock
teach.body: Formally, the HESI A2 Reading section has 55 items (50 scored) with a recommended 60 minutes, built from passages of roughly 250-500 words, each followed by a set of questions. That is about 65 seconds per item, including reading time. Plain English: you cannot afford to read the passage closely once per question. You read it once for the big picture, then go back only to the exact spot each question needs.

(1) Dehydration is a common reason older adults end up in the hospital, and it often develops quietly. The sense of thirst weakens with age, so many older people feel no urge to drink even when their bodies need fluid.

(2) Other changes add to the risk. Some common medicines, such as water pills prescribed for high blood pressure, increase the amount of fluid the body loses. Trouble walking can make trips to the bathroom harder, and some people drink less on purpose to avoid them.

(3) The early signs are easy to miss: dark yellow urine, a dry mouth, dizziness when standing and, in some cases, new confusion. Family members may mistake that confusion for ordinary aging.

(4) Simple habits help. Offering a glass of water with every meal and every medicine, keeping a filled bottle within reach and serving water-rich foods such as soup and melon can raise daily intake without anyone having to feel thirsty.

teach.h: Scenario: Devon works the set in under six minutes
items: Skim (2 min): Devon Brooks, applying to an RN program, jots gists: (1) thirst fades; (2) medicines and mobility add risk; (3) signs are easy to miss; (4) habits help.
'What is the main idea?' From the gists: older adults dehydrate easily and quietly, but simple habits help. No rereading needed.
'According to the passage, why do some people drink less on purpose?' Scan for 'on purpose' in paragraph 2: to avoid hard trips to the bathroom.
'As used in paragraph 3, the word signs most nearly means...' Read paragraph 3: indications of a problem, not posted notices.
'It can be inferred that a relative who sees new confusion...' Paragraph 3 implies it may be dehydration, not just age. Devon picks the modest option and moves on.

rows.label: Look at
values: A key word, number or name

teach.caption: Skim once at the start; scan as often as the questions need.

teach.h: Match the key word, then the qualifier
teach.body: Pick the stem's most specific word (a name, number or unusual term) and scan for it or a synonym: the stem may say 'older residents who cannot leave home' where the passage says 'homebound seniors'. Then read the whole sentence and check every qualifier: weekday or weekend, before or after a change, adults or children. Most wrong options are real details that answer a slightly different question.

teach.text: Time traps: rereading the whole passage for every question; spending two minutes on one item when the set still has four to go; and trusting an option because it copies the passage's exact words (copied wording with a changed meaning is a classic distortion). Make your best supported choice and keep moving.

items: HESI A2 Reading: 55 items, 60 minutes recommended, about 65 seconds per item including reading.
Skim the passage once for paragraph gists; answer big-picture stems from the gists.
Classify each stem, then go straight to the named paragraph or the key word.
Scan for the key word or a synonym, read the whole sentence, and match every qualifier.
Do not reread the passage per question or let one item eat the set's time.

summary: You can now work a full HESI A2 passage set at pace: skim once for gists, classify each stem and go straight to the spot it needs. You can also locate stated details by scanning for key words and synonyms and checking every qualifier.

A.q: The HESI A2 Reading section has 55 items with a recommended time of 60 minutes. About how much time does that allow per item, including reading?
options: About 65 seconds
About 30 seconds
About 2 minutes
About 90 seconds
A.why: 60 minutes = 3,600 seconds; 3,600 / 55 is about 65 seconds per item, and that includes the time spent reading the passages.

whyNot.1: Too little: 30 seconds per item would need only about 28 minutes for the section.
whyNot.2: Too much: 2 minutes per item would need about 110 minutes.
whyNot.3: Too much: 90 seconds per item would need about 83 minutes.

A.q: A question asks, 'According to paragraph 3, why did the clinic add Saturday hours?' What is the most efficient first step?
options: Reread the whole passage from the start
Scan paragraph 3 for the word Saturday
Skim the first sentence of each paragraph
Pick the option using the most passage words
A.why: The stem names the paragraph and gives a key word. Scan paragraph 3 for 'Saturday', then read the sentence around it for the reason.

whyNot.0: Rereading the whole passage wastes time when the stem names paragraph 3.
whyNot.2: Skimming first sentences suits main-idea questions, not a stated reason.
whyNot.3: Options that copy passage words are often distortions; this is not a strategy.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Seasonal allergies follow the calendar. Trees release most of their pollen in early spring, grasses in late spring and early summer, and ragweed from late summer into fall.

(2) Pollen counts also rise and fall with the weather. Warm, dry, windy days carry the most pollen, while a steady rain washes much of it out of the air.

According to the passage, when does ragweed release most of its pollen?
options: In early spring
In late spring and early summer
From late summer into fall
On warm, dry, windy days
A.why: Scan paragraph 1 for 'ragweed': it releases pollen 'from late summer into fall'.

whyNot.0: Early spring is when trees release most of their pollen.
whyNot.1: Late spring and early summer are the grass season.
whyNot.3: This describes the weather that carries the most pollen, which answers a different question.

B.q: Which question type usually sends a test taker to one named paragraph rather than to the whole passage?
options: The main idea of the passage
The best summary of the passage
The author's primary purpose
A word's meaning as used in paragraph 3
B.why: 'As used in paragraph 3' names the exact place to read; substitution happens there.

whyNot.0: The main idea covers every paragraph, so it comes from the paragraph gists.
whyNot.1: A summary must cover the whole passage.
whyNot.2: The primary purpose is judged from the whole passage.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) A county health survey asked 1,200 adults about their sleep.

(2) Among adults who worked night shifts, 61 percent said they slept fewer than six hours on a typical workday. Among day workers, the figure was 22 percent. Nearly half of all respondents said they used a phone in bed.

According to the passage, what percentage of day workers reported sleeping fewer than six hours on a workday?
options: 22 percent
61 percent
About half
39 percent
B.why: The qualifier is 'day workers': the passage gives 22 percent for that group.

whyNot.1: 61 percent belongs to night-shift workers, a different group.
whyNot.2: About half is the share of all respondents who used a phone in bed.
whyNot.3: This is the difference between the two groups (61 - 22), which the question does not ask for.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Hospital volunteers at Mercy General must complete a four-hour orientation.

(2) After orientation, new volunteers shadow an experienced volunteer for two shifts before working on their own. Volunteers under 18 may serve only at the gift shop and the information desk.

According to the passage, what must new volunteers do after orientation?
options: Work two shifts on their own
Shadow a volunteer for two shifts
Complete a four-hour orientation
Serve at the information desk
B.why: Paragraph 2: after orientation, new volunteers 'shadow an experienced volunteer for two shifts'.

whyNot.0: Copied words, changed meaning: the two shifts are spent shadowing, before working on their own.
whyNot.2: The orientation comes before, not after.
whyNot.3: This applies to volunteers under 18, not to all new volunteers.

C.q: A test taker has spent two minutes on one inference question in a six-question set and is still torn between two options. What is the best move at HESI pace?
options: Reread the entire passage once more
Skip the rest of that passage's items
Pick the better-supported option and move on
Choose the option using more passage words
C.why: At about 65 seconds per item, two minutes is already double the budget. Choose the option the passage supports more strongly and protect the time for the remaining items.

whyNot.0: A full reread costs another two minutes and puts the rest of the set at risk.
whyNot.1: Skipping several answerable items loses more points than one hard item.
whyNot.3: Copied wording is a distortion signal, not a sign of the right answer.

C.q: A 400-word health passage is followed by six questions. Which plan best fits the HESI A2's time?
options: Read the passage closely twice, then answer
Read each question, then reread the passage
Answer the word item before any reading
Skim for gists in two minutes, then answer
C.why: About 6.5 minutes covers the whole set. A two-minute skim for gists answers the big-picture stems and tells you where to scan for the rest.

whyNot.0: Two close readings use most of the set's time before a single answer.
whyNot.1: Rereading per question multiplies reading time by six.
whyNot.2: A word item still needs its paragraph, and the gists help the other items.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) When the Fairview mobile clinic began in 2019, it visited four rural towns once a month.

(2) In 2022, a state grant paid for a second van, and visits increased to twice a month. Last year, the clinic added two more towns to its route, and it now offers dental cleanings as well as checkups.

According to the passage, how many towns does the mobile clinic serve now?
C.why: Four towns at the start, plus two more added last year: 4 + 2 = 6. The qualifier 'now' rules out the 2019 figure.

whyNot.1: Four was the number in 2019, before the route grew.
whyNot.2: Two is the number of towns added, not the total.
whyNot.3: This doubles the towns because of the second van; vans and visits are not towns.

reteach.title: A grocery run with a list
reteach.question: You have six items on a shopping list and twenty minutes. Do you walk every aisle for each item? How is a smart grocery run like a HESI A2 passage set?

blocks.body: A smart shopper glances at the aisle signs once when she walks in (the skim). Then for each item she goes straight to the right aisle (the paragraph), finds the shelf (the sentence) and checks the label: 16 ounces, low sodium (the qualifiers). Walking the whole store for every item is rereading the passage for every question: you run out of time before the list is done.

blocks.text: The can next to the one you want looks almost the same. Check the label, just as you check every qualifier in the stem before choosing.

explain.body: 55 Reading items in a recommended 60 minutes is about 65 seconds per item, reading included. A 400-word passage takes about 2 minutes to skim, leaving about 45 seconds for each of six questions.

test.q: At HESI A2 pace, about how long should a 400-word passage with six questions take, including reading?
options: About 3 minutes
About 6.5 minutes
About 12 minutes
About 20 minutes
test.why: Six items at about 65 seconds each is about 6.5 minutes, with the reading time built in.

whyNot.0: Three minutes leaves almost no time for six answers after reading.
whyNot.2: Twelve minutes is nearly double the pace; the section would run far over 60 minutes.
whyNot.3: Twenty minutes would use a third of the section on one passage.

explain.body: Skimming reads lightly for the gist of each paragraph; scanning hunts for one word, number or name. Skim the passage once at the start, then scan for each detail question.

rows.label: Find a dose on a label

test.q: Which task calls for scanning rather than skimming?
options: Getting a sense of what a long report covers
Deciding whether an article is worth reading
Finding the dose listed on a medicine label
Previewing a chapter's headings before class
test.why: Finding one specific fact, such as a dose, is a scanning task.

whyNot.0: A sense of what a report covers is the general idea, which calls for skimming.
whyNot.1: Judging whether an article is worth reading needs its general idea: skimming.
whyNot.3: Previewing headings is a skimming step for an overview.

explain.body: Before you look for the answer, decide what kind of question it is. Whole-passage stems (main idea, title, summary, purpose) come from your gists. Located stems (a named paragraph, a key word, a number) send you to one spot.

test.q: A question asks, 'Which conclusion is best supported by paragraph 4?' Where should the test taker look first?
options: The title and the first sentence
The final sentence of the passage
Every paragraph in order from (1)
Paragraph 4, read in full
test.why: The stem names paragraph 4, so read that paragraph in full and choose the conclusion it best supports.

whyNot.0: The title and opening point to the passage's topic, not to paragraph 4's evidence.
whyNot.1: The last sentence may sit in a different paragraph; the stem names paragraph 4.
whyNot.2: Reading every paragraph wastes time when the stem names one.

explain.body: Scan for the stem's most specific word or a synonym, read the whole sentence around it, and check each qualifier: day, group, time, before or after a change.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) The Lakeside flu clinic runs on weekdays from 4 to 7 p.m. at the public library.

(2) On Saturdays it moves to the high school gym and runs from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. Children under 18 must come with a parent.

According to the passage, where can a person get a flu shot on a Saturday morning?
options: At the high school gym
At the public library
At the Lakeside clinic office
At the library after 4 p.m.
test.why: Scan for 'Saturdays': the clinic moves to the high school gym, 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., which includes the morning.

whyNot.1: The library is the weekday site, the wrong qualifier.
whyNot.2: No clinic office is mentioned as a site.
whyNot.3: 4 p.m. at the library is the weekday schedule.
